rules.questionsAreFixed: Questions are seeded, never LLM-generated. The LLM produces documents only.
rules.conditionalBranching: Deferred - not in MVP. dependsOnQuestionId reserved but unused.
rules.revise: Editing an individual answer re-runs generation for the affected fields only.
rules.generationOrder: All 4 phases are answered first, then MRD -> PRD -> Business Plan, because bp.product_weaknesses depends on the other two.
rules.noMarketEstimatesAsked: The founder is asked for objectives and decisions only — never for a market size, a conversion rate or a customer lifetime. Those are derived from published sources so that the plan has an independent view to validate his goals against. Retired for this reason: p2q3 (reachable market), p4q3 (expected conversion), p4q6 (expected lifetime).
rules.twoViewsThenAVerdict: Every document carries two figures for the same quantity: what the founder is aiming at, and what the sources support. The Business Plan closes with a verdict comparing them.
rules.revenueIsABand: The revenue objective is one question with two bounds (p4q8), not two questions. A founder asked separately for a target and a walk-away figure gives two unrelated numbers; asked for a band he has to say what "worth doing" actually spans. p4q11 was folded in as the lower bound.

phases.name: Idea & Strategic Goal
phases.description: Establishes what the product is, who it serves, and what success means.

phases.name: Market & Audience
phases.description: Establishes who the user is and where they are. How big the market is, is derived from published statistics — never asked.

phases.name: Product & Features
phases.description: Translates market needs into scoped, prioritised functionality.

phases.name: Your Objectives
phases.description: What you want the product to achieve and what you can spend to get there. No market estimate is requested here; every figure the plan rests on is derived and then compared against these goals.

questions.text: In one or two sentences, what does your app do and who is it for?
questions.helpText: This single answer seeds the Vision, the Problem statement and the Product Vision. Be concrete: what the user does, and what they get.
questions.placeholder: An indoor navigation app that guides shoppers to specific products inside large stores and malls.

questions.text: Which category best describes it?
questions.helpText: Selects which benchmark file the app is permitted to cite. If your category has no sourced data, figures will be marked 'unvalidated'.

questions.text: What is the single most important outcome in your first 12 months?
questions.helpText: Sets the OKR frame. Everything downstream is judged against this.

questions.text: Which platforms will you launch on?
questions.helpText: Affects acquisition-cost benchmarks — reported iOS and Android CPIs differ materially.

questions.text: What is your unique advantage over anyone else solving this?
questions.helpText: The UVP. If you cannot name one, that is itself a finding the Business Plan should report.
questions.placeholder: Existing maps stop at the building entrance; we map the interior and sell placement to store owners.

questions.text: Who is the user, and who actually pays? (If different, describe both.)
questions.helpText: Functional (user) vs economic (buyer) segments. In an ad- or B2B-funded model these are rarely the same person.
questions.placeholder: Users are shoppers navigating a mall. Payers are store owners and mall operators buying placement.

questions.text: Which geographic market are you launching in first?
questions.helpText: Used to pull the population, urbanisation and internet-penetration figures that the market size is calculated from. You are never asked how big the market is — it is derived.

questions.text: Name up to three existing products users could use instead.
questions.helpText: Queried against the App Store to retrieve real pricing, ratings and category. 'Nothing' is a valid answer — and usually a warning sign, not a moat.
questions.placeholder: Google Maps, Waze, individual mall apps

questions.text: What do users do today, and why is it unsatisfying?
questions.helpText: The unsatisfied need. Describe the current workaround, not the ideal.
questions.placeholder: They wander, ask staff, or give up. Large venues have no reliable indoor wayfinding.

questions.text: Which group are you aiming at?
questions.helpText: This narrows the market from everyone in your country down to the people you actually serve. Every option is filtered using a published national statistic — none of it is estimated. Choosing two assumes the groups overlap independently, and the documents say so.

questions.text: List the core features a first version must have.
questions.helpText: Only what is required for the product to function at all. Everything else belongs in the next question.
questions.placeholder: Indoor map rendering, live position, search for a store or product, turn-by-turn route.

questions.text: List features you want but could launch without.
questions.helpText: Feeds the RICE prioritisation and the phased rollout plan.
questions.placeholder: Accessibility routing, offline maps, promotions from nearby stores, multi-floor transitions.

questions.text: What is the single most important thing a user must be able to do?
questions.helpText: The primary value proposition, expressed as an action. Activation metrics are defined against this.
questions.placeholder: Find a specific product inside a venue and be walked to it.

questions.text: How will you know the product is working?
questions.helpText: Selects which KPI families the PRD reports, benchmarked against your category where data exists.

questions.text: What is the biggest technical risk or constraint you already know about?
questions.helpText: Surfaced honestly in the Business Plan's weakness section rather than discovered after build.
questions.placeholder: Indoor positioning without GPS needs venue-by-venue surveying — it does not scale on its own.

questions.text: How will the product make money?
questions.helpText: Business model is reported to predict retention more strongly than category — this drives which benchmarks apply.

questions.text: What do you intend to charge, per paying customer per month?
questions.helpText: A decision you control, not a prediction. It is checked against what comparable apps actually charge on the App Store and against the published category ARPU, and any large divergence is flagged.

questions.text: What will you spend per month to build and run this, excluding marketing?
questions.helpText: Engineering, infrastructure, tools and services. Marketing is asked separately because it is the number that determines how many users your money can actually reach.

questions.text: How will the first users find you?
questions.helpText: Paid channels are costed against published cost-per-install benchmarks; organic channels are not, and the plan says so.

questions.text: What will you spend per month on reaching new users?
questions.helpText: Advertising, app-store ads, paid placements — anything whose job is to bring users in. This is divided by the published cost-per-install for your category to work out how many users your money actually buys. Enter 0 if you plan to grow only organically.

questions.text: What monthly revenue would make this worth doing?
questions.helpText: Give a band, not a point. The lower figure is the revenue below which you would stop — your floor. The upper figure is what you are actually aiming at. Both are goals, not predictions: the app works out independently what your category, market and budget support, and reports where that lands against your band.

questions.text: How many active users would you count as success?
questions.helpText: Again a goal, not an estimate. Judged separately from the revenue goal, because reach and money can fail independently — and knowing which one fails tells you what to fix.

questions.text: By when do you want to have reached those two goals?
questions.helpText: The projection runs month by month to this horizon, and the verdict is issued at it. A goal that is unreachable in 6 months is often reachable in 24 — the app says which.

demoSet.description: The 5 questions answered LIVE on Demo Day. The seed project pre-fills the rest; these 5 are cleared and re-entered on stage. Chosen to touch all three documents, exercise text/select/multiselect/number input, and drive both the derivation chain and the verdict.
demoSet.remainingAnswers: Pre-filled from seed-project.json (indoor navigation). Visible and editable, but not typed on stage.

business_plan.note: Provision is a rule of thumb - renders unvalidated.
Auto-filled: which answers, benchmarks and API calls were used.

mrd.derivedFrom: p2q5 + p3q1, restated as 'The user shall...'

mrd.note: Unvalidated where no sourced figure exists.
Unvalidated for categories lacking ARPU data.

prd.note: Crash-free/ANR/cold-start targets currently UNVALIDATED - no sourced figures.

calculationLayer.description: Deterministic arithmetic. The LLM never computes these - it receives the results and narrates them.
inputs: p4q8 objective_revenue band: floor and target (goals, judged — never inputs to a projection)
p4q9 objective_users (goal, judged — never an input to a projection)

formulas.note: DERIVED, not answered. Was reachable_market * conversion_pct, both of which the founder used to supply. Both questions are retired.
Applied only for app-store distributed models. commission_pct from benchmarks (30 standard / 15 reduced).
Compared against the category ARPU benchmark; divergence >2x is flagged.
cpi_benchmark from the category file. UNVALIDATED if the category has no CPI figure.
Compared against the sourced 1.5x viability floor. The 3:1 target is unvalidated and must not be asserted.
Infinite if price is 0 - reported as 'not applicable for this model', never as a number.
Lifetime is now DERIVED from the category retention or churn benchmark. It was answered (p4q6), which made LTV an assumption resting on a guess.
Judged against a band. Below the floor is a stop; inside the band is a proceed; above the target beats the goal. Reported with the ratio to each end.
Judged separately from revenue: reach and monetisation fail independently.
Back-solve. What the acquisition budget would have to be for the goal to hold, all else equal. One of three levers reported; the others are price and horizon.
Back-solve on price, compared against competitor prices so the reader can see whether that price is one anybody in the category actually charges.
Null when the projection never reaches it inside 60 months, which is itself the answer.

guardrails: Any formula whose inputs include a placeholder benchmark returns null and renders 'unvalidated'.
Division by zero returns null with an explanation, never Infinity or NaN.
Every computed value carries the confidence tier of its weakest input.
Results are passed to the LLM as pre-computed facts. The LLM must not recalculate them.

A lifetime the user asserts is an assumption, never a measurement. It is reported alongside what the published retention benchmark implies, so an unsupported figure is visible rather than silently multiplied into LTV.
An objective is never an input to a projection. It is only ever compared against one.
Back-solved levers are reported as what would have to be true, never as a recommendation to assume it.

derivations.note: Average lifetime = 1 / monthly churn, with D30 retention read as monthly retention. NOT used as expected_lifetime_months. D30 retention counts installs still opening the app, not customers still paying — a different population — so it is used only to cross-check the answer to p4q6. Unvalidated where the category has no sourced D30 figure. churn_monthly_pct would be preferred if any vertical published one; as of the 2026-08-10 review, zero of sixteen do.

comparisons.note: Flags when the answered lifetime diverges more than 2x from benchmark_implied_lifetime_months. Reported as a divergence, never as a correction: the benchmark measures a different population and may legitimately not apply.
Divergence greater than 2x from the category ARPU benchmark is flagged.
Judged against the sourced 1.5x campaign viability floor only.

derivationLayer.description: How the market is sized without asking the founder. Each step names the source it reads. A step whose source is missing renders unvalidated and stops the chain below it — it is never bridged with an assumption.

chain.note: Total addressable people in the market the founder named (p2q2).

sources: World Bank (per segment, see segments below)
chain.note: segment_filter comes from p2q6. Two segments multiply, which assumes independence — a caveat the documents must carry. platform_share comes from p1q4.
The budget-constrained route. Unvalidated where the category has no sourced CPI.

chain.expr: sum over months of (installs_affordable_monthly * store_conversion_pct/100 * surviving_fraction(month))
chain.note: Cohorts accumulate and decay. This is the serviceable obtainable market, derived — it replaces the retired p2q3.
The independent view the founder's objective (p4q8) is judged against.
A budget-derived SOM larger than the SAM means the market, not the budget, is the binding constraint. Reported, never silently clamped.

Registered businesses (B2B).note: Coverage is patchy across countries. Renders unvalidated where the country has no value.

guardrails: No step may be bridged by an assumption. A missing source stops the chain and the documents say where it stopped.
Two segments multiply only under a stated independence assumption, printed as a caveat.
A derived SOM exceeding the SAM is reported as a market-bound result, never clamped in silence.
The derived figures and the founder's objectives are kept in separate fields all the way to the document. They are never averaged or reconciled — they are compared.
